name: [Boost].UT (boost-ext/ut)
baseline: GoogleTest 1.10.0, Catch2 2.10.2, Boost.Test 1.71.0, doctest 2.3.5 (compile time of test code using each framework)
workload: Compile and run synthetic test programs generated from templates: 0 tests (include only), 1 test with 1,000,000 asserts, 1,000 tests in one file, and a 100-file suite of 10,000 tests with 20,000 to 40,000 asserts (with and without STL use), built by clang 9 and gcc 9 in default, -g and -O3 modes.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Compiles 5x faster because it doesn't introduce a new type for each lambda' (design claim, no number attached) and 'faster to compile and execute than similar frameworks'. Benchmark results exist only as bar-chart images; values read off the charts (approximate): include-only compile about 0.4 s for UT vs about 1.0 s Boost.Test, 0.8 s GoogleTest, 5 to 16 s Catch2, 1.3 to 3.3 s doctest. 1,000 tests in one file, clang9 default: UT about 1 s vs about 7 s Boost.Test, 4.5 s GoogleTest, 5.5 s Catch2, 2.2 s doctest. 100-file suite with asserts and STL, clang9 default: UT about 55 s vs about 195 s Boost.Test, 130 s GoogleTest, 110 s Catch2, 50 s doctest; gcc9 -O3: UT about 230 s vs about 730 s Boost.Test, 430 s GoogleTest, 705 s Catch2, 270 s doctest. Execution of that suite (unoptimized): UT about 0.04 s vs about 1.1 s Boost.Test, 0.1 s GoogleTest, 1.8 s Catch2, 0.5 s doctest.
compiler_and_flags: Public bench.sh: clang++ and g++ (gcc 9.2.0 toolchain) with -std=c++2a; variants default, -g and -O3 -DNDEBUG; UT-only extra runs with -stdlib=libc++. Catch2 built with CATCH_CONFIG_FAST_COMPILE, doctest with DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS, Boost.Test and GoogleTest as static libraries.
tradeoffs: Needs C++20 (GCC 9+, Clang 9+, Apple Clang 11+, MSVC 2019+). Single header or C++20 module, macro-free API built on concepts, source_location and designated initializers, so error messages and idioms differ from GoogleTest, Catch2 and doctest; the project is a testing framework, not a build tool, so its place in the compile-caching category is a loose fit for 'faster to compile test code'.
caveats: Numbers come only from bar-chart PNGs in the benchmark repo (no tables), so every figure above is read off a chart and approximate. The CPU model and machine are not stated anywhere, so the run falls short of tier A. The benchmark repo (cpp-testing/ut-benchmark) is the UT README's own linked benchmark, i.e. first-party. Versions are from 2019 (UT 1.1.0, GoogleTest 1.10.0, Catch2 2.10.2, doctest 2.3.5, Boost.Test 1.71.0, gcc 9 and clang 9); newer releases of every framework exist and were not re-measured. On the large suite doctest is roughly on par with UT for compile time (about 50 s vs 55 s with clang9; doctest slower with gcc9 -O3 at about 270 s vs 230 s), so UT's compile-time lead is clear against Boost.Test, GoogleTest and Catch2 and small or none against doctest. The '5x faster because it does not introduce a new type for each lambda' line in the README is a design claim with no benchmark behind it. UT's own test registration style differs from the baselines, so workloads are not byte-identical test programs.

name: Bazel
baseline: GNU Make 4.3 with default built-in rules (also measured: Make with --no-builtin-rules --no-builtin-variables, and Ninja 1.11.1, both of which beat Bazel)
workload: Third-party overhead benchmark: N simulated modules (50 to 100,000) whose build rules only touch 0-byte files, measured as full build, incremental build (a few files changed) and null build (nothing changed), parallelism 4.
claimed_speedup: Bazel's own README claims only 'fast and incremental builds' (no numbers). Third-party table, x86_64, 100,000 modules: incremental build Bazel 61.911 s vs recursive Make (default rules) 692.201 s and single Make 292.019 s (about 11x and 4.7x, derived from page data); null build Bazel 20.193 s vs 688.101 s and 285.583 s (about 34x and 14x, derived from page data). At 5,000 modules: incremental 4.040 s vs 22.408 s / 24.813 s; null 1.091 s vs 22.236 s / 24.473 s. NEGATIVE results in the same table: Ninja is faster at every size (100,000 modules: incremental 10.358 s, null 7.073 s, full 407.131 s vs Bazel 61.911 s, 20.193 s, 1381.402 s), Make run with --no-builtin-rules is also faster than Bazel for incremental and null builds (9.486 s and 7.816 s recursive at 100,000 modules), and Bazel's full build is slower than every Make and Ninja variant (e.g. 82.779 s vs 28.723 s Make and 6.079 s Ninja at 5,000 modules).
compiler_and_flags: No compiler involved (rules touch 0-byte files); tools run with no arguments plus Make with --no-builtin-rules --no-builtin-variables; GNU Make 4.3, Ninja 1.11.1, Bazel 8.0.1 on the Arm runs, Bazel version recorded as 'no_version' on the x86_64 runs.
hardware: x86_64 run: 4 CPUs, 7G RAM, Linux 6.8.0-48-generic (Ubuntu 22.04); Arm run: aarch64 4 CPUs, 7G, Linux 6.8.0-1018-raspi (kernel name suggests a Raspberry Pi); CPU model not stated; runs dated 2025-02-10/11
tradeoffs: JVM server process: 350 to 500 MB resident in these runs and 310 MB to 1 GB of output-base disk even for empty modules; slow cold full build; steep learning curve (BUILD/Starlark files, many options); hermetic sandboxed actions with remote cache and remote execution, whose benefits this benchmark does not exercise. Output lands in the user cache directory, not the source tree.
caveats: The benchmark is synthetic and measures pure build-tool overhead: no compiler runs, so it says nothing about real C or C++ compile and link wall-clock time or about remote caching and execution, which are Bazel's main speed levers. Bazel only wins against Make run with default built-in rules (the benchmark's own results show Make drops to Ninja-like times with --no-builtin-rules) and only on incremental builds from about 5,000 modules and null builds from about 1,000 modules (on Arm at 1,000 modules Make is still faster); at small sizes (50 to 100 modules) Bazel's full build is about 10 to 22 s vs 0.04 to 0.23 s for Ninja and Make, and Ninja beats Bazel in every row. The measurement is by a single maintainer repo with 5 stars (GPL-3.0 benchmark code, last commit 2025-02-28); CPU model is not stated, so it cannot be tier A. The Bazel version is not recorded on the x86_64 runs. The Bazel repo itself carries no Make or Ninja comparison; the Bazel 'fast' claim is first-party and unquantified.

name: C++20 modules instead of header inclusion (Alibaba Hologres case)
baseline: header-based includes (#include); whether precompiled headers were in the baseline is not confirmed
workload: Compile time of Alibaba's Hologres mainline code base after moving from header inclusion to C++20 modules (per search-result snippet of the Alibaba Cloud blog; the page itself could not be opened).
claimed_speedup: Alibaba reports C++20 modules cut Hologres compile time by 42% (blog title '42% Boost in Compilation Efficiency! A Practical Analysis of C++ Modules'); snippet says modules have run on the Hologres mainline for more than a year and a half. A snippet also mentions an import-std test of about 0.03 s, 'an order of magnitude' better than headers (unverified).
stars_or_usage: Used on the Hologres mainline (Alibaba Cloud data warehouse), per the blog snippet
tradeoffs: Needs a compiler with working C++20 module support and a build system that scans module dependencies; the technique is a language feature, so there is nothing to copy except the migration approach described in the post.
caveats: Snippet only: www.alibabacloud.com failed to resolve (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND) in this session, so the numbers, compiler, flags, hardware and baseline details come from WebSearch result summaries, not from the page. Vendor blog about a product the vendor sells, so tier C at best. Hologres is a commercial Alibaba Cloud product with no public source repository found, no benchmark code is public, compiler and flags are unknown, and it is unclear whether the 42% covers full or incremental builds, whether it includes the standard library, or whether a precompiled-header baseline was used. Independent reports in the same search put module speedups between 10% and 50% and one LLVM forum thread reports build times increasing after migrating to modules, so the figure is plausible but project-specific. Listed 'repo_url' in the assignment is the blog page, not a code repository.
